## Overview {-}

### Description {-}

This workshop introduces you to the `r Biocpkg("PSMatch")` R and Bioconductor
package. As you will see, the package also depends on another Bioconductor
package called `r Biocpkg("PTMods")` and we also highly suggest using the 
`r Biocpkg("Spectra")` package for plotting spectra. All three packages are part
of the [R for Mass Spectrometry](https://www.rformassspectrometry.org/) package
series and you are welcome to learn more about this project by visiting its
corresponding website.

In short, `PSMatch` is a Bioconductor package for handling proteomics
identification data whilst `PTMods` handles post-translational modifications
(PTMs). You are encouraged to run the code interactively as I will present each
section.

By the end of this workshop, you will be able to import, explore, filter, and
visualise peptide-spectrum match (PSM) data; model peptide-protein
relationships using adjacency matrices; and handle PTM annotations in a
principled, reproducible manner.

### Pre-requisites {-}

- A conceptual understanding of shotgun proteomics: what a peptide
  is, what a mass spectrum is, and what a database search does. 

### Suggested readings {-}

- The `r Biocpkg("PSMatch")` package vignettes, accessible via
`browseVignettes("PSMatch")`. 
- The pre-print available on the OSF platform:
[PSMatch: an R/Bioconductor package to explore proteomics identification
data.](https://doi.org/10.31219/osf.io/62v9p_v3). Note that the package has
gone through quite a few changes since.

### Participation {-}

As I already mentioned, you are welcome to follow along with me. Code is
provided in full, no typing from scratch is required. The code can be fetched
from [this GitHub repo](https://github.com/guideflandre/PSMatchWorkshop).

### Workshop goals {-}

- Understand the structure of peptide-spectrum match data and how it is
  represented in R using the `PSM` class.
- Recognise the problem of shared peptides and protein ambiguity, and
  know how adjacency matrices and connected components help address it.
- Appreciate the diversity of PTM annotation conventions and know how
  to convert between them and enumerate modified sequences.
- Understand the sometimes lacking confidence in identifications and as such,
  the importance of validating PSMs.

### Learning objectives {-}

- Import an identification data file into R and inspect the resulting `PSM`
  object.
- Apply the standard filtering steps (decoy removal, rank filtering,
  shared-peptide filtering, fdr filtering) individually and via `filterPSMs()`.
- Build an adjacency matrix and connected components from PSM data
  and visualise a protein group as a bipartite graph.
- Convert a PTM annotation between *deltaMass*, *unimodId*, and *name*
  formats using `convertAnnotation()`.
- Apply fixed and variable modifications to a peptide sequence and
  calculate theoretical fragment ions that account for those
  modifications.
- Plot spectra by including annotations based on the identification.
- Improve the confidence in a PSM using `validatePSM()`, built based
  on spectral and identification metrics.


# Who is the package for and when to use it ? {-}

The package is built for proteomics practitioners who want to explore their
identification data or peptide-spectrum matches.

<img src="../images/workflow.png" width="600"/>

In mass spectrometry-based proteomics, after generation of raw spectra, you
would typically apply a database search or _de novo_ sequencing to identify
which peptide could have been at the origin of each MS2 spectrum. The
identifications, or so-called Peptide-Spectrum Matches (PSMs) are the results
of this search.

<img src="../images/dbSearch.png" width="600"/>

`PSMatch` is the package you reach for once a search engine has matched your
spectra to peptide sequences and you want to explore, filter, and annotate
those identifications. Note that different search engines will generate
different file types and identifications. Still, a few file contents remain a
standard amongst search engines: 

1. The **peptide** or sequence matched
2. The **rank** of the PSM for a same spectrum
3. The data **origin**
4. The scan number or **spectrum identifier**
5. The **associated proteins** for that PSM
6. Its search engine **score**
7. The **FDR** associated to that PSM based on its given score.

# Loading and exploring PSM data {-}

## Installing and loading the package {-}

The packages used in this workshop are all available from Bioconductor.
`PSMatch` and `PTMods` are constantly being improved and some functionalities
that are presented in this workshop are not yet available through the latest
Bioconductor release versions (1.16.0 and 1.0.0 respectively). 

To install the correct versions for this workshop, use:

```{r installVlatest, eval = FALSE}
remotes::install_github(c("rformassspectrometry/PSMatch@validatePSM", 
                       "rformassspectrometry/PTMods"), build_vignettes = TRUE)
```

For the other packages, the usual install can be used:

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
if (!require("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install(c("PSMatch", "PTMods", "Spectra", "MsDataHub",
    "TargetDecoy"))
```

```{r load, message = FALSE}
library(PSMatch)
library(PTMods)
library(Spectra)
library(TargetDecoy)
```

## Example data {-}

In this workshop, we will use different data available through the 
`r Biocpkg("MsDataHub")` package. 

`psmBoekweg` and `spBoekweg` are subsets of the `Boekweg2022` data. The subsets
are also bundled in the `PSMatch` package as of version `1.17.2`. For more
information on the data, you can run `?MsDataHub::Boekweg2022`.

We will also use an mzIdentML file from the `MsDataHub` package. This file
contains search results from a TMT-labelled Erwinia carotovora sample acquired
on an Orbitrap instrument.

```{r datafile}
## Load psmBoekweg, the identification file as a result from a database search
data("psmBoekweg")
```

## The `PSM()` constructor {-}

The `PSM` class is a lightweight extension of the `DFrame` class from 
`r Biocpkg("S4Vectors")`: it is a tabular object where each row is one PSM. You
can build a `PSM` object from a `data.frame` using the required column names by
using the `PSM()` function.

```{r psm-load}
## Create a PSM/spectrum identifier
head(psmBoekweg$pkey <- paste0(basename(psmBoekweg$filename),
                               sub("^.+scan=", "::", psmBoekweg$scannr)))

(
    psms <- PSM(x = psmBoekweg,
        spectrum = "pkey",
        peptide = "peptide",
        protein = "protein",
        decoy = "label",
        rank = "rank",
        score = "hyperscore",
        fdr = "spectrum_q")
)
```

Calling the `PSM` object returns a quick overview of its contents. There are
10000 rows or PSMs, with a total of 42 columns or features. All 10000 PSMs have
a unique spectrum identifier and there are 1823 decoys in this dataset. The
ranks for all PSMs are equal to 1.

Note that a different dataset might not have decoys or different PSM ranks, it
would then have multiple PSMs with a same spectrum identifier. For instance,
the following mzid file from `MsDataHub`:

```{r id-load}
f <- MsDataHub::TMT_Erwinia_1uLSike_Top10HCD_isol2_45stepped_60min_01.20141210.mzid()
(
    id <- PSM(x = f,
        spectrum = "spectrumID",
        peptide = "sequence",
        protein = "DatabaseAccess",
        decoy = "isDecoy",
        rank = "rank",
        score = "MS.GF.RawScore",
        fdr = "MS.GF.QValue")
)
```

You can call or store the initially defined PSM variables using
`psmVariables()`.

```{r psm-explore}
(psmVar <- psmVariables(psms)) ## defined PSM variables used in the package
(idVar <- psmVariables(id)) 
names(psms)
```

## Decoy and target hits {-}

A typical database search should also provide decoy PSMs: the hits that provide
an estimate of the false discovery rate (FDR). The data are loaded *as-is*,
without any filtering. 

We can filter out these decoys that don't hold any biological meaning other
that helping to estimate the FDR:

```{r psm-decoy}
psms
(psmsNoDecoys <- filterPsmDecoy(psms))
```

The `r Biocpkg("TargetDecoy")` package is a useful Bioconductor package to
analyse the quality of the target-decoy distribution in your data. It provides
functions to plot a histogram of the disctributions as well as a
percentile-percentile plot, which measures when those distributions differ.

Note, a typical dataset should have a bimodal distribution for the targets and
a distribution for the decoys that fits the first peak of the targets'
distribution well. High-confidence PSMs are those targets that distinguish
themselves from the decoys through a higher search engine score. The more
dubious target hits are those that dissociate themselves from the decoy
distribution too early. See `browseVignettes("TargetDecoy")` for more
information on the topic.

```{r tdc}
evalTargetDecoysHist(data.frame(psms),
    decoy = "label", score = "sage_discriminant_score",
    log10 = FALSE, nBins = 80
)
```

## Multiple matches per spectrum {-}

A search engine can return more than one candidate sequence for each spectrum.
The table below shows that several spectra have up to 5 candidate matches for
the TMT dataset.

```{r psm-multi}
table(table(id$spectrumID))
```

Let us inspect a concrete example: scan 1774 has 4 matches, all assigned to the
same peptide sequence but to four different proteins.

```{r psm-scan1774}
i <- grep("scan=1774", id$spectrumID)
data.frame(id)[i, c(idVar["spectrum"], "sequence", "DatabaseAccess", "rank")]
```

This is known as a *shared peptide*: a peptide whose sequence is present in
more than one protein. We will come back to this in the adjacency matrix
section.

## Reducing to one row per spectrum {-}

If you want to retain all matches but collapsed into one row per spectrum
(storing multiple values as lists within each cell), use `reducePSMs()`.

```{r psm-reduce, warning = FALSE}
dim(id)
idReduced <- reducePSMs(id, id$spectrumID)
dim(idReduced)

## Each spectrum now has exactly one row
anyDuplicated(idReduced$spectrumID)

## The multiple values are stored as lists in each cell
j <- grep("scan=1774", idReduced$spectrumID)
data.frame(idReduced)[j, "DatabaseAccess"]

## You can check if a PSM object is reduced or not with `reduced()`
reduced(idReduced)
```

# Filtering PSM data {-}

`filterPsmDecoy()` was already mentioned, but there are 3 other handy filtering
functions available in `PSMatch`:

- `filterPsmRank()` that filters out PSMs whose rank is greater than 1.
- `filterPsmShared()` that filters out peptides that match to more than one
protein: the so-called shared peptides.
- `filterPsmFdr()` that filters PSMs based on a specified FDR threshold. By
default, the threshold is set at $5\%$.

The convenient `filterPSMs()` wrapper applies all filters above except the
`filterPsmFdr()`:

```{r filters}
id |> filterPSMs() 
psms |> filterPsmFdr(FDR = 0.01)
```

# Protein ambiguity and adjacency matrices {-}

The simple table representation of PSM data hides an important structure: the
*relationship* between peptides and proteins. 

## Describe peptides|proteins {-}

For a more in depth understanding of the peptides and proteins in your data,
you can call `describePeptides()` and `describeProteins()`. The message
displayed in the console defines the peptide and protein compositions in terms
of shared and unique peptides. 

Out of the 10000 PSMs, 9254 are uniquely identified peptides, out of which 4021
are uniquely linked to a protein. The rest are shared peptides, i.e. peptides
that may stem from 2 or more proteins. 

Out of 11727 proteins, 2254 have only 1 peptide linked to them. 9186 have
shared peptides only and 287 have a mix of unique and shared peptides.

```{r describe}
describePeptides(psms)
describeProteins(psms)
```

Two proteins that share a peptide are connected and PSMatch models this
relationship using adjacency matrices and connected components.

## Reload and filter {-}

Let us start from a freshly loaded, filtered PSM table (keeping rank-1
non-decoy hits but *not* removing shared peptides, so we can explore the
sharing).

```{r adj-load}
psmsFiltered <- psms |> filterPsmDecoy() |> filterPsmRank()
data.frame(psmsFiltered[1:10, psmVar[c("peptide", "protein")]])
```

## Building the adjacency matrix {-}

Let's visualise the relationship between peptides and proteins as an adjacency
matrix instead of within a table.

An adjacency matrix has **peptides as rows** and **proteins as columns**. A
value > 0 at position *(i, j)* means peptide *i* was observed for protein *j*.
A binary matrix uses 1/0 whilst a weighted matrix uses the count of PSMs or its
given search engine score. If a peptide was observed multiple times, the sum of
scores is used. Because we defined the `"score"` variable when constructing the
`PSM` object, the weighted matrix with summed scores is built by default.

```{r adj-build}
adj <- makeAdjacencyMatrix(psmsFiltered)
dim(adj) ## peptides × proteins
adj[1:5, 1:5]

## Set score = NA for counts only and binary = TRUE for a binary matrix
adj <- makeAdjacencyMatrix(psmsFiltered, score = NA)
dim(adj)
adj[1:5, 1:5]
```

Let's use the matrix with counts for now. Notice that the matrix is sparse:
quite a few peptides map to only one protein as shown with
`describePeptides()`. Some entries are > 1 because the same peptide sequence
was observed multiple times (different charge states, modification sites, ...).

## Connected components {-}

The full adjacency matrix is too large to interpret directly. Instead, we
decompose it into **connected components**: subsets of peptides and proteins
that are connected to each other (directly or through shared peptides) but
isolated from the rest of the matrix.

```{r cc-build}
cc <- ConnectedComponents(adj)
cc
length(cc)
```

We have many connected components. Let us look at what kinds exist.

```{r cc-types}
## Single protein, single peptide (simplest case)
connectedComponents(cc, 2)

## Single protein, multiple peptides (well-identified protein)
connectedComponents(cc, 22)

## Multiple proteins sharing a single peptide
connectedComponents(cc, 1)

## Multiple proteins, multiple peptides (most complex)
connectedComponents(cc, 11)
```

For interesting cases where a group of proteins that are connected through
shared peptides exist, we can visualise and understand the structure of these
groups.

## Visualising adjacency matrices {-}

Let us find connected components with at least three peptides and three
proteins.

```{r cc-large}
head(largeCC <- which(nrows(cc) > 2 & ncols(cc) > 2), 15)
dims(cc[head(largeCC, 15)])
```

We will use component 1049 to illustrate `plotAdjacencyMatrix()`. Proteins are
represented as blue squares, peptides as white circles. An edge connects a
peptide to every protein it maps to.

```{r adj-plot}
cx <- connectedComponents(cc, 1049)
cx
plotAdjacencyMatrix(cx)
```

Immediately we can see that peptide `` is shared across all four
proteins. If we removed that peptide, the component would split into smaller,
simpler groups.

## Prioritising components for inspection {-}

When there are many complex connected components, we need a way to prioritise
which to inspect first. `prioritiseConnectedComponents()` computes a set of
metrics (including its dimensions, row and col sums maxima and minima, its
sparsity and the number of communities and their modularity that quantifies how
well the communities separate) for each component and ranks them.

```{r cc-prioritise}
cctab <- prioritiseConnectedComponents(cc)
head(cctab, 15)
```

A principal component analysis of these metrics can reveal groups of
similar components or outliers that deserve attention first. Note that
trivial components are ignored.

```{r cc-pca, message = FALSE}
library("factoextra")
fviz_pca(prcomp(cctab, scale = TRUE, center = TRUE))
```

# PTMods: handling modifications {-}

Before continuing, I will briefly introduce the functions from the `PTMods`
package that `PSMatch` is dependent on.

## PTM annotation styles {-}

As I already mentioned, different search engines and databases generate
different PSM file formats. They also use different syntaxes for annotating
modifications within a peptide sequence. `PTMods` handles all of them
transparently. The three (currently supported) annotation styles are:

```{r ptm-styles-table, echo = FALSE}
ptmStyles <- data.frame(
  Style=c("`deltaMass`", "`unimodId`", "`name`"),
  Example=c("`M[+15.994915]PEPTIDE`", "`M[UNIMOD:35]PEPTIDE`", "`M[Oxidation]PEPTIDE`"),
  Description=c("Mass shift in square brackets", "Unimod accession number", "Human-readable PTM name"),
  SearchEngine=c("Sage", "(MSFragger)", "MaxQuant")
)

knitr::kable(ptmStyles, align="lll")
```

The `convertAnnotation()` function converts between these styles. The
conversion is based on an up-to-date `data.frame` built from the
[unimod.org](https://www.unimod.org/modifications_list.php?) website.

```{r ptmods-convert}
## Name → deltaMass
convertAnnotation(
    "M[Oxidation]PEPTIDE",
    convertToStyle = "deltaMass"
)

## deltaMass → name
convertAnnotation(
    "M[+15.995]PEPTIDE",
    convertToStyle = "name"
)
```

## Adding modifications {-}

Adding modifications can be done one of two ways: through
`addFixedModifications()` or through `addVariableModifications`.

### Fixed modifications {-}

By default, carbamidomethylation is added as a fixed modification. Other PTMs
can be added using the `fixedModifications` parameter which accepts a named
vector. The annotation style is up to the user and can be changed later down
the line using `convertAnnotation()`.

```{r ptmods-fixed}
addFixedModifications(
    "SCALITDGR",
    fixedModifications = c(C = "Carbamidomethyl")
)
```

Fixed modifications can also target the N-terminus or C-terminus of a peptide,
or a specific residue position.

```{r ptmods-fixed-nterm}
## TMT labelling of the N-terminus (mass 304.207 Da)
addFixedModifications(
    "SCALITDGR",
    fixedModifications = c(Nterm = 304.207)
)
```

```{r ptmods-fixed-pos}
## Fluoro modification at position 1 only
addFixedModifications(
    "SCALITDGR",
    fixedModifications = c("Fluoro"),
    pos = 1
)
```

### Variable modifications {-}

`addVariableModifications()` returns *all* sequences that can be formed by
placing the modification on zero, one, or more of the eligible residues.

A sequence with 2 potential modification sites will thus generate 4
peptidoforms.

```{r ptmods-variable}
addVariableModifications(
    "MPEPTIDE",
    variableModifications = c(M = -15.995, T = "Phospho")
)
```

The number of sequences grows exponentially with the number of modifiable
residues. The `maxMods` parameter caps the maximum number of simultaneous
modifications.

```{r ptmods-variable-maxmods}
addVariableModifications(
    "MPEPTIDE",
    variableModifications = c(M = -15.995, T = "Phospho"),
    maxMods = 1
)
```

## Stripping modifications {-}

`getCanonicalSequence()` removes all modifications and returns the bare amino
acid sequence. This is useful for grouping modified and unmodified forms of the
same peptide.

```{r ptmods-canonical}
getCanonicalSequence("[+304]-M[Oxidation]PEPT[UNIMOD:21]IDE")
```

# Fragment ions and spectrum visualisation {-}

Fragment ions are the basis of MS2-based peptide identification. When a peptide
is fragmented, backbone bonds break and produce a series of ions. For a peptide
of length *n*, the b-ion series covers fragments from the N-terminus ($b1$ to
$b_{n-1}$) and the y-ion series covers fragments from the C-terminus ($y1$ to
$y_{n-1}$).

PSMatch provides `calculateFragments()` to compute theoretical fragment masses,
and `plotSpectraPTM()` to overlay them on the observed spectrum, essentially
annotating the observed spectrum based on the provided sequence for that PSM.

## Load raw and identification data {-}

We merge raw spectra with identification results. The raw mzML file is also
available from `MsDataHub`.

```{r frag-load, message = FALSE}
data("spBoekweg")

head(spBoekweg$pkey <- paste0(basename(spBoekweg$dataOrigin),
                              sub("^.+scan=", "::", spBoekweg$spectrumId)))

## Merge by spectrum identifier
sp <- joinSpectraData(spBoekweg, psms,
    by.x = "pkey",
    by.y = "pkey"
)
sp

## Set 'sequence' variable equal to 'peptide' but with converted PTM notation
sp$sequence <- convertAnnotation(sp$peptide, "name")
```

## Isolate a single PSM {-}

We focus on scan 6570, which was matched to `r sp$sequence[27]`.

```{r frag-select}
sp6570 <- filterPrecursorScan(sp, 6570)
## Both MS1 and MS2 spectra, only MS2 has an identification
(sek <- sp6570$sequence) 
```

## Calculate theoretical fragment ions {-}

`calculateFragments()` takes a peptide sequence and returns a `data.frame` with
the m/z, ion type, charge, and position of every theoretical fragment. By
default, carbamidomethylation of cysteines is applied automatically.

```{r frag-calc}
frags <- calculateFragments(
    sek[2],
    addCarbamidomethyl = FALSE
)
frags
```

The columns are:

- **`mz`**: theoretical m/z of the fragment ion.
- **`ion`**: ion label (e.g. `b3`, `y5`).
- **`type`**: ion series (`b` or `y`, or `a`, `c`, `x`, `z`).
- **`z`**: charge state.
- **`pos`**: sequence of the fragment for that mass.
- **`peptide`**: the precursor peptide sequence.

## Fragment ions with PTM enumeration {-}

Of course, `calculateFragments()` supports the same PTM annotation styles
supported by `PTMods`. A typical workflow would include the addition of PTMs
through the use of `addVariableModifications()` or `addFixedModifications`.
Passing this vector of generated sequences to `calculateFragments()` then
produces its own set of fragment ions, traceable by the `peptide` column.

```{r frag-ptmods}
(
    varSeqs <- PTMods::addVariableModifications("ATK", 
        variableModifications = c(T = "Phospho"))
)

calculateFragments(varSeqs, verbose = FALSE)
```

## Visualising the spectrum with `plotSpectraPTM()` {-}

`plotSpectraPTM()` overlays the theoretical fragment ions on the observed MS2
spectrum. It also draws a delta-mass plot (observed minus theoretical m/z
values for each matched fragment) to assess matching quality, and a sequence
coverage diagram showing which b- and y-ions were matched.

```{r frag-plot-basic}
plotSpectra(sp6570[2]) ## raw spectrum
```

```{r frag-plot-ptm}
plotSpectraPTM(sp6570[2])
```

The figure has multiple sections:

1. The top includes the Universal Spectrum Identifier (USI) and an optional
   title as well as a direct visualisation of which b- and y-ions were matched
   along the sequence.
2. The main plot is the actual annotated spectrum. The fragment intensities are
   displayed as relative intensities to the base peak. The base peaks can be
   recognised as it is annotated with the raw intensity value. The matched
   peaks can be coloured by the user, as well as other typical plotting 
   parameters.
3. An optional (but useful) plot is the `deltaMz` plot that shows the
   difference between the observed and theoretical mass-over-charge values of
   the matched peaks.

Adjusting the `ppm` parameter helps fine-tune the accepted range for matching
peaks. In any case, the closest peak to the theoretical m/z will be recorded
only if it falls within this `ppm` range.

In the following plot, increasing the `ppm` parameter to 150 made it match 2
more fragments (the y3_ and b5 ions). However, such a high ppm does not
encourage us to trust these matches.

```{r frag-plot-ppm}
plotSpectraPTM(sp6570[2], ppm = 150)
```

We can compare the match quality with and without Oxidation for that
PSM to confirm that the modification is genuine.

```{r frag-plot-compare}
spComp <- sp6570[2]
spComp$sequence <- getCanonicalSequence(spComp$sequence)
plotSpectraPTM(spComp,
    variableModifications = c(M = "Oxidation"),
    deltaMz = FALSE,
    asp = 2/1,
    main = c(
        "Scan 6570, no oxidation",
        "Scan 6570, with oxidation"
    )
)
```

The spectrum with oxidation shows more matched fragments, confirming that the
methionine indeed modified.

The function becomes very useful for cases where an identification is not quite
convincing. Plotting these different annotated spectra with and without PTMs,
whilst checking the `deltaMz` plot helps validating a PSM.

# Validate PSMs {-}

Until now, we have handled data as they come out of a search engine. In this
section, we will try to improve our confidence in a PSM based on spectral and
identification metrics.

Basic metrics are typically calculated and given by the search engines. Think
about the number of matched fragments, the longest fragment matched, the score,
the FDR, ...

With `validatePSM()`, we can add some metrics that are not reported in any of
the search engines we have used so far. The function is actually a wrapper for
other functions that calculate these metrics. For more on those, see
`?validatePSM`. 

```{r validatePsms, warnings = FALSE}
scans_seq <- precScanNum(sp[!is.na(sp[["sequence"]])])
sp <- filterPrecursorScan(sp, scans_seq)

(
    res <- validatePSM(sp[1:20], 
        peptideVariable = psmVar["peptide"], 
        fdr = psmVar["fdr"])
)
```

Some metrics need a modification to be relevant, others don't. In any case,
these metrics can be added to the initial PSM object by matching their
`spectrumId`.

```{r addMetrics}
psm_df <- as.data.frame(psms)
combined <- merge(psm_df, res,
    by.x = "scannr", by.y = "spectrumId",
    all.x = FALSE
)
```

An example of these metrics is `checkOverlap()`. This functions evaluates
whether the matched b-ions and y-ions together cover the entire peptide
sequence. If not, a gap is detected. `checkOverlap()` returns `FALSE` when such
a gap is detected and `TRUE` when b- and y-ions jointly cover the sequence with
overlap.

```{r checkOverlap}
sp_ms2 <- sp[msLevel(sp) == 2L & !is.na(sp$sequence)]

checkOverlap(sp_ms2[10])
plotSpectraPTM(sp_ms2[10])
```

In the example above, it `checkOverlap()` serves as a ringing bell that shows
an alarming identification for which the amino acids within that identified gap
have never been matched. It could be interesting to re-apply a search with
variable modifications. For instance with phosphorylation on serine or
oxidation on methionine. 

For a more in depth use of these metrics, we suggest parsing through the
corresponding vignette (see `vignette("validatePSM", package = "PSMatch")`).


# Summary {-}

With this, we have covered the main features of PSMatch (as well as PTMods):

1. **Loading PSM data** : `PSM()` reads mzIdentML files or `data.frame`
   instances into a tidy `DFrame`-based object with full access to all search
   engine output.

2. **Filtering** : `filterPsmDecoy()`, `filterPsmRank()`,
   `filterPsmShared()`, and the convenience wrapper `filterPSMs()`.

3. **Adjacency matrices and connected components** :
   `makeAdjacencyMatrix()`, `ConnectedComponents()`,
   `plotAdjacencyMatrix()`, and `prioritiseConnectedComponents()`
   provide a principled framework for exploring protein ambiguity.

4. **PTM handling** : PTMods gives access to the Unimod database and
   provides `convertAnnotation()`, `addFixedModifications()` and
   `addVariableModifications()` for
   annotation conversion and modification addition

5. **Fragment ions** : `calculateFragments()` computes theoretical
   b/y (and other) ions whilst `plotSpectraPTM()` overlays them on observed
   spectra with delta-mass diagnostics.

6. **Validate PSMs** : `validatePSM()` uses different checks and metrics to
   validate an identification.
